title: IP address, MAC address and ARP

videos.script: Lesson two used an address and did not explain it. A number that names a machine, we said, and left it there on purpose. {{owed}} Here is what that number actually is, and why one of them was never enough. A machine has at least two addresses at any moment, they are given out by different people, for different reasons, and they change on completely different schedules. {{two}} One is burned into the network card at the factory and never changes. The other is handed to you by whatever network you happen to be on, and is gone when you move. {{contrast}} That sounds like waste until you ask what each one is for. The permanent one answers which card on this wire; the temporary one answers where in the world. A card that moved between countries and kept the same worldwide address would be a card nobody could route to. {{why}} By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at an address and say whether it is yours, whether it is local, where it came from, and what happens to it on the way out of your house. {{title}}

Your house has one public address. Count the things in it that are online right now — the phones, the laptops, the television, the speaker, the doorbell. All of them are talking to the internet, and between them they have one address. {{house}} How? Here is the router, and here is the table it keeps. {{table}} A laptop sends a request. It leaves with the laptop's private address and a source port. The router rewrites both: the address becomes the public one, and the port becomes a number the router picks. Then it writes a line in the table — this public port belongs to that laptop, on that port. {{rewrite}} The answer comes back addressed to the public address and that port. The router looks up the line, rewrites the two numbers back, and hands it to the laptop. Thirty devices, one address, thirty thousand available ports to keep them apart. {{return}} And now the part that matters. Watch what happens when somebody OUTSIDE tries to start a conversation. {{inbound}} A packet arrives for the public address, on some port. The router looks in the table — and there is no line, because no line is created until somebody inside sends something first. There is nothing to rewrite it to, so it is dropped. {{no-row}} That is NAT, and it is why you cannot simply run a server at home, why two people behind different routers cannot call each other directly without help, and why every device you own can reach the internet while nothing on the internet can reach any of them. {{consequence}} It is also, accidentally, the most widely deployed firewall in the world. Nobody designed it as one. It became one because a table with no row is a packet with nowhere to go. {{firewall}}
